Lay the pelt out flat. Never fold a fresh hide.
Spit on the thread before you thread it. It makes the knot hold. Spit is good for many things.
A good skinner works in silence. A great one works in song. Our Master sings, at night.
Thin the edges before you stitch. A seam too thick shows through the fabric.
Wear a hide a week to learn how it sits. Wear it a month to learn what it knew.
The salt must be coarse. Fine salt burns. Don't ask how we found out.
The brine barrel sat too warm in the sun last night. The batch is ruined.
When the needle breaks, bury the needle. A broken one remembers the pain it caused.
I wore Marcus last winter. Marcus was agreeable. He insisted on writing letters home.
We have an unspoken rule. Nobody asks what the other was called, before.
My name this week is Peren. Don't use it too often.
Which of us is the real Dolan? We're three. We have all been Dolan.
A new face takes a week to settle. Until then I dream the other man's dreams.
Mirror, mirror. I was sure I smiled. The mirror says otherwise. Perhaps it isn't my mouth.
I looked in the water this morning and nobody I knew looked back.
Hm hm hm. Hm hm. Don't mind me. It's one of the songs from the road.
The wind has a tune today. A cheerful one. I think someone has fed it.
I do like the lullaby the last woman sang. I hum it for the new ones. They calm down.
Someone is whistling behind us on the road. Nobody in our party whistles.
Do you hear that? Behind us. Tick, tick. A little bell. A little bell on a child's shoe.
She cried for two days. On the third she sang. We let her go on for a while.
The Master is in a mood. When he's in a mood, we take orders in writing.
Someone has been sleeping in the good coat. I'll find out who.
The patrol brought a Shek last night. Such a lot of hide. The Master is thrilled.
Eight pairs of gloves on order for the Cities. Eight. Do they know what they're buying?
We lost a man at the Pits last week. His face is still out there somewhere. Somebody ought to fetch it.
My coat has been talking in its sleep. The pocket says a name. I can't make it out.
A stranger fell in with us at dawn asking for work. We gave him the apron.
The wardrobe is full again. I do like to go through it of an evening, saying good night.
I have named every coat. Poor Henry. Poor Mirelle. Poor, poor Ansel.
They tell me I'm mad. I have a letter saying so, signed by four doctors. I wear two of them.
A new voice came in today. It is a little high. I think I will keep it for the mornings.
Nobody knows what I look like. Not even me. I stopped consulting the mirror years ago.
A tanner in Stack found his own face pinned to a drying frame. Same mole. Same crooked brow. He sold the shop that week.
The tanner kept it, you know. The face. Wrapped it in cloth and slept next to it for a month. Then he vanished too.
He recognised the scar on its lip. Got that scar falling off a cart when he was nine. A stranger sent the hide in, with a note: kindly appraise.
They asked him what he did with it. He said he buried it. His wife said he put it on.
The tanner said the hide was beautifully worked. Not a hair wrong. He said that was the worst part.
It came in a crate marked for the Cities. Inside, a face and a receipt. Paid in full. His own name on the line.
Heard about the tanner who found his own face on a frame. Nobody says which town. Everybody swears they knew him.
I heard a tanner opened a shipment and it was his own skin, tidy and cured. He nailed up the shop and walked north.
A tanner somewhere south found his face in a delivery. He hasn't been the same. He wears a hood now, even at supper.
There's a story that a leatherman unpacked a bale and found his own mouth looking back at him. Smiling.
The Hub tanners all check their bales twice now. Do not ask me why. They are not laughing about it.
Some tanner got a face in his order. His own. The way I heard it, he laughed, then he didn't.
I met a man who swore a tanner got himself back in a crate. It's true. I heard it from three people who each saw it.
They say the skinners ship their work under false labels. Even to the men who made the leather.
Tanners are no longer allowed in the northern markets. They say they smell wrong.
A tanner saw his own face on a stranger at the market. He crossed the road. The stranger crossed with him.
At a wedding near the Pits the groom said all his vows, kissed the bride, shared the bread. Then the bride asked who he was.
The groom was wrong. Not in a way you could name. His smile didn't change when the music did.
His mother stared at him through the whole feast. She said afterwards she knew his hands, and these were somebody else's.
The real groom was found a week later behind the barn. Every guest remembers the groom smiling. The same smile, all night.
They had danced three songs before anyone noticed he cast no shadow of worry. He never frowned, never blinked at the toast.
He ate with his left hand. The groom was right-handed. That's how the bride knew.
Priests tell the story of a wedding where the groom came back wrong. They say it as a warning to marry in daylight.
A couple were wed under the Flame. In the morning the husband wouldn't enter the chapel. Said it was too bright for his eyes. They weren't his eyes.
A girl from the Valley says her cousin's husband had a stranger's face. A beautiful face. Too beautiful for a farmer.
Someone swapped the groom, and the whole village drank to him anyway. That's the part that frightens me.
The bride never told. She says she knew by the third night. She says she couldn't bring herself to say no to the smile.
I heard of a wedding where the groom was sewn in. Heh. I laughed. The man who told me didn't.
There is a tale about a bride who woke up next to someone else wearing her husband. She poured him tea. That is how you survive.
Everyone knows a groom is nervous. This one was calm.
A wedding party was found at the table, every guest still smiling. Nobody had touched the wine.
They say if your husband stops snoring, count the stitches behind his ears.
A child in Squin won't stop humming a dead man's song. A song nobody taught her. Her mother wept when she recognised the words.
The girl hums in the dark. The song is a slow one, a farewell. The man who wrote it was found skinned in the Pits in the spring.
She never learned it from anyone. She only started the night after a patrol came through. Her mother burned the girl's blankets.
The child sings it in a grown man's low voice when she thinks no one is listening. Her mother has stopped checking on her at night.
I sat with the girl for an hour. She knew my name. I had never told her my name.
She asks about the boots. Always about the boots. Where did the boots go? Who's wearing them?
There's a child who hums a song she can't have known. The priests were called. They left halfway through the hymn.
A kid in the Valley sings a lullaby that belonged to a soldier killed in Skinner's Roam. Nobody taught her. She just opens her mouth and out it comes.
A farmer's daughter hums a dead man's tune. Her father says it's the wind. Her mother says it's the stranger who stayed the night.
A boy was found alone on the road humming. They fed him and he stopped. Not one of the patrons was brave enough to ask whose song.
The song is a work song, they say, and the child can't stop. She keeps time against her ribs, like she's sewing.
A little girl sings a song she shouldn't know. Everyone says it happens.
The kid hums a ballad that died with its composer, and the composer is not the only thing that went missing.
I heard a child singing in the market and a man ran off. He told his wife later it was his brother's song. His brother is a year in the grave.
Remember the lullaby your mother sang? Imagine a stranger's child singing it, in your mother's voice.
There's a child who hums only when it rains. The songs aren't hers. She seems quite happy to carry them.
They leave the boots. Always the boots, side by side at the roadside, neat as a shop window. Nothing else.
We found a pair of boots by the dry well. Laced. Still warm inside. Nobody wanted to be the one who looked up.
A whole caravan, gone. Twelve pairs of boots at the crossing, set in a row. Whoever did it took care to leave the laces tied.
You see a pair of boots on the Pits road, you turn round. I have turned round three times.
A woman left her boots outside the Skinhouse door. Neatly. Like a guest. We never found out whether she walked in willingly.
Why boots? I think it's a message. Or a fashion. Or the only part they don't want.
In the Roam they leave the boots. Walk past a pair and keep walking. Don't pick them up. Don't even look at the laces.
Scouts tell me a pair of boots on a ridge means somebody finished measuring. Don't go closer.
My brother found boots at the edge of Skinner's Roam. Good boots. He wore them home. He hasn't been quite himself since.
A road marked by boots. The tribes have their totems, the Nation has its flame.
Never trade for boots you can't account for. A cobbler in the Hub paid for his carelessness. Ask what he found inside.
They leave the boots behind. Nobody says what they take instead. It's better that way.
Folk say if you find boots on a trail, with socks still in them, don't lace them up. You won't be the first to try.
Every desert has a legend. Ours is a pair of empty boots walking toward you. Please do not tell me how it ends.
Boots at a crossroads. Not a body. Not a bone. Just boots. The scavengers won't touch them. That's how you know.
I bought a pair at a bargain once. A merchant warned me. I took them back and he didn't charge a penny.
A coat walked into the Hub market, bold as brass, and bought six loaves. It hummed while it paid. The baker hasn't eaten since.
I saw a man in a long coat at dusk. The coat moved before he did. I don't know which of them was in charge.
The new coat at the cloth stall looked at me. I swear it. It had eyes in the lining. Pretty ones. Brown.
It was cut so well I couldn't see a seam. The tailor said it was made to fit, then went quiet. The fit was too good.
Someone sold a coat in the Cities last winter. Lined with fine skin. A woman bought it and wore it for a week.
I touched the sleeve. It was warm. Not warm like wool. Warm like someone had just taken their arm out.
There are coats in the northern markets that no one dares to touch. They're dyed the wrong colour.
A merchant tried a coat on in the shop. He is still wearing it. Nobody has been able to get close enough to ask.
A coat on a hook in the Valley inn turned its head when the door opened. The innkeeper burned it.
They say if your coat is warmer than the weather, take it off. Take it off slowly. Don't look at the inside of the collar.
I don't buy secondhand coats. Not after what happened to the last owner of mine. His face was in the hem.
There's a coat that walks the roads. If you pass it, nod politely and don't look at the hands.
A woman wore a lovely coat to market and the market left. Quietly, one by one, with their goods.
Fine coat, said the stranger, and walked off in mine. I found it hanging in a tree three days later.
The skin trade has wardrobes the size of villages. And the coats go out to market on their own two feet.
My uncle owned a coat that sighed in the night. He sold it on.
At the Pits gate a man called out in my sister's voice. My sister is a month's walk away. I didn't open the gate.
It knocked three times, soft, and called my name in my dead father's voice. I locked every bolt and sat with a knife till dawn.
My wife heard her mother outside the door, crying for help. Her mother has been dead for six years. She went out. I never saw her again.
They can do any voice they have swallowed. They stand outside and call. Don't answer.
A watchman said the voices come at the second hour, always friendly. They know your name, where you were born. They know your favourite song.
The voice said please. Just please. It had my brother's lisp. I almost opened. Then I remembered he was buried.
Shekfolk on the border say a voice called from the dark in the tongue of a warrior long dead. Four men went to meet him.
A priest in the Valley says the voice at the door was his mother's. He prayed against it. It answered, in her words, in his prayer's cadence.
If you hear your name called at night, count to forty before answering. If it's still calling, you know.
The mercenary camp near the Roam keeps a watch word. Not for the enemy. For voices that don't change when the word does.
A girl said the man at her window had her father's voice. Her father was beside her, holding her hand.
Someone knocked and spoke in the voice of a dead friend. That's all anyone will say.
They steal voices out there. Nobody has proven it.
I was told never to answer a voice at night that knows your first name. I have survived thirty years on that rule.
Never open to a kind voice after dark. It's the unkind ones you can trust.
A traveller swore he heard his wife call him from the dark. She was in the wagon with him, asleep. He swears the voice was sadder than hers.
A Cities caravan left the Pits road with eleven guards and arrived with twelve. The twelfth was very polite.
The guard captain says he doesn't recall hiring the extra man. The extra man ate, drank, and kept watch.
After a week the captain noticed that the twelfth guard had worn three different faces. Each handsomer than the last.
The merchants checked the roll at the gate. Twelve names. They had paid for eleven. The twelfth signed in their own hand.
Our caravan master drew a chalk line down the middle of the wagon and made us all cross it. The twelfth wouldn't.
One by one the guards stopped speaking, and when we reached the Hub they all had the same expression. It was the twelfth who was crying.
There's a caravan in the Nation that carried one more than it started with. The priests sprinkled holy water.
A mercenary told me the sign: a new man who knows the jokes but not the faces. Watch his laugh. It trails a heartbeat behind.
A trader says count your guards every morning, and count their shadows. Skin has no weight to cast one.
The Shek patrols stopped letting wagons through at dusk. The reason is a story about an extra man, and a missing child.
A guard captain told me the dead man in his unit signed for the pay. In his own hand.
A caravan was found whole on the Skinner road, all hands at their posts. No one answered. The goods were untouched and the bulls were calm.
A trader said his guards had one more every night and one less every morning. It balanced out, in the end.
The Traders Guild now pays double to those who travel in pairs. Pairs can't be quietly replaced.
A caravan came out of the Roam with its numbers right. Its tally of names was wrong.
I saw a wagon train return to the Hub with all its drivers smiling. Not one of them thanked the gate guard.
A man in a grey apron stopped me at a well and asked politely if he could measure my arm. I let him. I don't know why.
He had a tape the colour of old bone. He took my wrist, my elbow, the spread of my hand. He said thank you and left. I haven't slept since.
A stranger asked the barman for my size. The barman said he didn't know. The stranger said he would find out.
The measuring man comes to town twice a year. He is gone by sundown. Whoever he thanks does not come to supper.
He said I had a fine hand, steady, even. A craftsman's hand. I thanked him. He said no, thank me, for your cooperation.
It's the tape I remember. Cool, slightly damp. And the numbers written in dark ink. Nobody had told me my own numbers before.
A merchant was approached in a market by a courteous fellow with a tape. He's lucky. He said no. Most of them say yes.
Never allow a stranger to measure you. It's the first step. The rest is only craft.
I've heard the clerks in the Hub keep a sheet of measurements pinned inside a drawer. Nobody remembers whose they are.
A man with a tape followed a caravan for two days. He measured the horses. Then he measured the drivers.
A Shek warrior on the border says they asked her height, her age, and whether she was travelling alone.
A tailor stopped me in the road to say I carried myself well. I walked on faster than I have ever walked.
Be wary of any man who looks at you like he's measuring a grave.
A friendly stranger asked to measure my neck. He called it a courtesy.
Funny thing about the measuring men. They never haggle. They never argue. They simply nod and write.
The tailors who follow caravans aren't always tailors. Count their fingers.
A pair of gloves went on sale in the Hub, so fine you could read through them. The buyer wept when he put them on. One ring was still on the finger.
The glover said they came from the northern road. He said the hands that wore them first were exceptional. A scribe's hands, or a surgeon's.
A woman in the bar showed me her new gloves. She was very proud. The nails inside the fingertips were painted pink.
My brother bought gloves from a stranger. They fit him perfectly. The next morning his own hands were on the table, perfectly folded.
Gloves with a scar across the palm. A man in Stack swore it was his father's. He buried them, then found them in his coat.
There's a tailor that sells gloves for a month's pay. I asked why so dear. He said, the pairs are matched. I didn't ask what that meant.
Priests warn against second-hand gloves. They say the last wearer's fingers might remember.
A glove dealer showed me his stock. The thumbs were different sizes. The sizes of my thumb and my wife's.
The Cities fill with fine gloves in winter. No one asks where the hands go in summer.
A noble in the Valley wears gloves in the temple. Nobody has seen his hands in years. A rumour says they aren't his.
Never trust a handshake from a man who won't take off his glove. Trust a man who offers you both.
A pair of gloves was found on the road, still warm. Fingers curled as if holding something. Nobody wanted to look inside.
There's a market in Skinner's Roam for gloves. The price is unusual. They're paid for in names.
I like gloves, but only new ones. Old ones have too much to say.
The farmer found a glove in his field, and a hand in the glove. It wasn't his own, but it fit.
A glover in the Hub told me his trade secret: the best ones come from the north, and never ask for a refund.
A slave came back from the Skinhouse. Well fed, well dressed, smiling. The slavers took him to market and he wept the whole way.
Our overseer went to sell a woman at the Skinhouse. He returned with a gift: a pair of gloves, soft as breath. Then he stopped speaking to us.
I was bought by a quiet man, taken south. They fed me. They bathed me. They measured me. I escaped the night before the fitting.
Word is, the worst ones are the slaves who return. They look healthy. They smile. They aren't the same ones who left.
The Skin boss pays best for the unmarked. No whip scars. No brand. We keep them unblemished, you see. Then we sell them.
A shackled man said the Skinhouse is the only market where the buyers say sorry. Always sorry.
Slave traders in the Holy Nation refuse to deal with the Skinned Ones. Not from morals. From fear of what they ask for.
I heard they pay triple for slaves who have never been hurt. A tidy price. A tidy trade. A tidy way to disappear.
A Shek slaver told me never to sell to a man who inspects the skin of your slaves with his fingers. He keeps a ledger of the sizes.
A woman bought free from the Skinhouse says the last thing she saw was a rack of faces, labelled by hand. Neat handwriting.
Free slaves do not talk about the cellar. They only touch their cheeks and look at their palms.
A rumour among the shackled: the Skinhouse is where the unlucky ones go. The kind who are made to look lucky first.
Never be the best looking slave in the pen. A man with a measuring tape will pick you.
Slaves whisper that the Skinhouse stands at the end of the Pits road. They say it has a fine garden. The roses grow very well.
I knew a slave bought by a polite man. He said the buyer thanked him for being so well kept. He didn't come back to the stall.
In the cage next to mine they sang about the Skinned Ones. A cheerful tune. They stopped when a quiet man came by.
A Shek warrior walked out of Skinner's Roam. The stripes on his face were right. The way he held his sword wasn't.
He answered to the right name. He knew the Shek greeting. His smile showed too many teeth.
His family knew. A Shek child notices what a warrior forgets: the old scar had moved to the other cheek.
Esata the Stone Golem
The Stone Golem's priests found him in a field, counting grass blades. He was very proud of his count.
His brother killed him on the road and wept at what was inside. Not a warrior. Nothing a Shek could name.
He spoke the oath without a single mistake. Too fluently. A true Shek stumbles over the word for honour.
The Shek say a warrior can wear a flatskin's face, but not their stripes. They're wrong. I've seen the proof.
A Shek patrol has orders to ask every returning scout one question. The answer isn't written down. It's a word they never speak aloud.
The Shek of the border are stricter than ever. Returning scouts are watched three days before they're allowed to sleep.
Their warriors won't share a tent with a man who sleeps too quietly. Real Shek snore like sandstorms.
I heard a Shek patrol came back from the Roam one man short and one man more. They killed the extra man at the gate. He was very polite about it.
Shekfolk tell the story of a warrior who came home from the Roam with stripes in the right places. His hounds howled all night.
The Kingdom says one of their own was worn like a cloak. They're proud, and say nothing.
A trader says a Shek bought the same hat twice in one week. Same man, different manners.
Honour is a hard thing to counterfeit. The Skinned Ones try anyway.
Stripes don't wash off, a Shek told me. I asked how he knows. He said they tried.
A woman at the Hub saw a stranger on the street and called out her son's name. He walked just like him. He stopped, turned, smiled.
She followed him for six streets, calling. He kept answering, 'Yes, Mother,' without turning. He knew her name. He didn't know her face.
She said it was the way he held his left shoulder. A weak one, from a childhood fall. This stranger wore the same ache, not the same man.
She stopped him and put her hand on his cheek. It was her son's skin, his mole, his freckle. She asked, 'Where's he?' The stranger said, 'I'm here.'
The guards say the woman won't eat now. She sits near the gate, watching men walk past, whispering their gaits to herself.
She asked where he got the scar on his chin. He said, 'You gave it to me.' She had. Her son was five. The stranger wasn't five.
A mother in the Valley swears her son came home, but wrong. He eats politely. He says please.
A woman tells it at the temple door: she recognised her son's walk in a pilgrim, followed him, and he didn't mind. He let her follow him to the fire.
People say it's a mercy to grieve the dead. It's a torment to grieve the living, who walk past you on the road wearing your child.
I know a mother who burns every stranger's coat she can reach. She says she's looking for a button. A blue one.
A shepherd's wife watched her husband return and said he was too tidy. He had never been tidy in his life.
A mother called out to a stranger by her lost child's name. The stranger turned and answered. I'd keep walking, if I were you.
They say a mother always knows her child. So do the skinners. That's why the faces get used elsewhere.
Never ask a returned traveller about his mother. He will answer, and the answer will be right.
A woman who lost her son keeps a lamp lit in the window. She says if he walks by in someone else's face, she will recognise the light in his eyes.
Some stories only mothers believe. They're usually the true ones.
Four of us found a camp in the Roam. Table laid for six. Five cups drunk. The sixth was full, and still warm.
The fire was lit, the stew simmering. Bedrolls, unslept. A tin plate set at every place, one more than there were bedrolls.
A camp with its tent flaps tied back neat. Everything folded. Everything tidy. The only thing out of place was the smell of soap.
At the camp, someone had laid out a set of clothes by the fire. Boots, belt, trousers, shirt, folded. A single cloth beside them, the right size for a head.
One of us said, count the plates. There were eight and we were seven. We left before we reached the last tent.
The camp was full of half-finished meals and I swear we heard a soft voice say, 'Do sit down.' None of us sat.
Nomad scouts won't stop near a camp laid with too many places. They say hospitality out there has a price, paid in one lump.
Our patrols avoid any fire that has been left burning with a tidy circle of stones around it. It means someone is waiting.
Hunters tell of a camp with a kettle always on, a chair always empty. The tea is excellent. The chair is a trap.
A bounty hunter found a camp with every lamp lit, every tent pitched, and nobody around. He stayed an hour. It cost him a friend.
Raiders report a camp that no one dared loot. It had everything. They say the stew was still hot after three days.
Drifters say if you ever find a camp with the fire still warm and the place settings laid, back out quietly and don't touch the stew.
A camp in the desert with a table for seven and six chairs. No one has ever asked who sits in the seventh.
Traders swear by the old rule: if there's more food than people, someone is still cooking.
A story goes that a whole squad vanished from a camp and left their boots and a note, thanking nobody for dinner.
In the Roam, the camps are laid out for guests. The guests are always the last to know.
A drone walked into the Hub speaking in a human voice, perfectly. It paid for water, bowed, thanked the seller.
A Hive soldier in the Cities spoke of its dead companions by name. Names of men. It said they were all gone, and wept in a clicking voice.
The Hivers are afraid of the Roam. A drone told me they lost a whole scouting party there. The drones came home with human faces drawn on their carapaces.
A Hiver tried to buy a coat. It insisted on feeling the stitching first, and then it hummed a sad little hum and left.
A drone at the gate whispered, 'Do not let the tall ones wear you.' It would not say who the tall ones were.
Somebody in the Skinhouse learned to cut a Hive carapace without breaking the antennae. The Hivers won't talk about it. They hum instead.
The tall ones in the Roam wear faces. We do not understand faces. We understand taking.
Our scouts went into the Roam and the Roam kept some. We don't send more.
A drone told the market it dreamt of a human hide. We don't speak of it.
The skinners learned to cut a carapace. We felt it. We felt the cut in all of us.
The Western Hive keeps drones away from the Roam. Not out of fear. Out of curiosity, which the Queen finds more dangerous.
A Hive prince told a trader that his people do not own faces. The skinners have been teaching them what a face is, and what it costs.
Savant
The Southern Hive would love the Skinhouse. If Savant ever falls, the drones will be in the halls within the hour.
A Hiver in the market told me it dreamt it wore a human hide. It woke humming a human song. It asked me to forget it.
Hivers don't hunt skinners for revenge. They do it for the chance to learn why anyone would want to be someone else.
A Hiver told me it dreamed of a house full of faces. It said it didn't want to go back to sleep.
I heard a drone sing a human lullaby. A drone can't know a lullaby. Someone taught it, and I don't like who.
Strange folk, the Hive. They say all drones are the same. The Roam proves them wrong, one carapace at a time.
A trader said he saw a drone in a human face, clicking softly. It nodded politely and walked on.
There's a Hive saying: the Queen has one face. The skinners have a thousand.
Savant
The bounty poster for Savant has no face. Clerks draw a smooth oval and write the sum beneath. Every artist who tried to sketch him quit.
Savant
A sketch artist drew Savant from three witnesses. Three drawings, three men. He tore them up and walked into the desert.
The poster says eighty thousand, then fifty thousand underneath. The clerks say both are right, and neither is enough.
A boy tried to claim the bounty with a sack of faces. The clerk asked him politely to leave. The boy left, but the sack stayed. It's still in the office.
The Cities refuse to draw a likeness. They're afraid the picture would look back.
On the poster, where the face should be, someone has pinned a scrap of leather. Nobody admits to it.
The Hub's bounty board has a poster with no face. Hunters touch it for luck. Then wash their hands.
Savant
A hunter told me he had a good lead on Savant, then pulled out his pocketbook. There was a lock of hair in it, in another man's colour.
The poster says he can be found on his throne or in his bed. It doesn't say what's under the sheets.
Hunters who go for the reward rarely come back. A few do, with different faces.
Eighty thousand cats. Think of it. Think of what you would buy. Now think of who you would have to be to spend it.
A wanted poster with no face hangs in half the guild halls. Never ask who tore the picture off.
The reward is enormous. Nobody has claimed it. Not for lack of effort.
A story goes that the poster was drawn by a man who saw him once. He drew the mouth only, very small, smiling.
I'll tell you the secret of the poster. The blank isn't a mistake. Look closer, it fits whoever's looking.
A bounty so high, a face so blank. They say it takes a particular sort of courage to put up that poster.

People think nobody inside the walls is still thinking. They are wrong, and I have the proof, though not on me.
They say the Holy Nation keeps its women quiet. Quiet isn't the same as empty.
I knew a Holy Nation woman once. She said less than anyone and remembered more.
Out of the Nation, you can carry words, goods or nothing at all. The nothing is the most dangerous.
Never ask a Holy Nation woman where she's going. She will tell you the truth, and it will be worse than a lie.
The Inquisitors have been asking after cords and knots. They will not say why.
A priest looked at a sleeve for a long time today. I don't know what he thought he saw.
I hear someone is asking questions near the women. No one answers them, and that is an answer too.
There was a search, and nothing was found, and everyone looked pleased about it. I do not trust that.
Somebody brought us a cord from inside the Nation. We haven't stopped talking about it.
A knotted cord reached us from inside. Each knot is a person. We read them all.
Whoever carried that cord out, we owe them. We just don't know how to say it.
We kept the cord. We didn't keep the carrier's name. We didn't need it.
Ronin cut marks in things. Hide, wood, their own arms, some of them. I don't ask which days they're counting.
I knew a ronin who said it was too quiet out here. I told him it wasn't, with the raptors about.
Some hive princes lose the hive and keep the habits.
A ronin doesn't sleep like we do. I have watched. He lies down and listens for something.
Some of the lost ones count. We don't know what they count.
The hive hears many things. It doesn't always hear the lost ones.
A lost one passed our way. He didn't stop. He looked like he was listening.
We do not speak of those who left. We notice them.
Hive ronin are strange company. Polite, careful, and never quite here.
I heard a ronin counting once, under his breath, over and over. It was the same number.
Never share a fire with a ronin unless you can stand silence. They give a lot of it.
A ronin told me he doesn't miss the hive. He said it three times.
Somebody carried a notched strip of hide to a hiver and the hiver took it without a fuss.
A ronin gave away his days and a hiver kept them. I'd like to have seen it.
I hear a stranger took a ronin's marks to the hive. People in my line of work don't do that sort of thing for free.
A ronin walked away lighter this week. I saw it.
An outsider brought a count to one of us.
A drone took marks from a stranger and did not ask for coin. We noticed.
We hold the days of one who left.
The hive keeps what it's given. It was given a count.
There are Shek who walk outside the Kingdom. We do not name them.
A Shek leaves the Kingdom and the Kingdom does not say a word. That is how you know.
Some who left will come home. Some won't. Some won't be asked.
Hrm. Outside the Kingdom a Shek is only a tall /FLATSKIN/ with horns. He knows it.
Shek do not forget. If one owes the Kingdom, he owes it until he dies. I would not carry his debt.
Shek mercenaries say they have no home, and then they look at the horizon the way they look at it.
A Shek will hold a grudge for longer than you'll live. A Shek will also hold a promise.
I knew a Shek who sold his sword to anyone but wouldn't sell his hide.
Never touch a Shek's leather. They know when it has been touched.
The Shek keep marks on things. I don't know what they mean.
I saw a Shek scrape a mark off a strip of hide for most of a night. He didn't look up.
Shek don't apologise. They sometimes leave a thing where you'll find it.
Something was returned to the Kingdom by a /FLATSKIN/'s hand. No one will say what. Everyone is quiet about it.
A strip of hide came back. The one who sent it isn't named.
A debt was paid by proxy. A Shek would have preferred to pay it himself.
We had a visitor with a hide. He left. We did not ask his name.
A traveller put a strip of hide in a Shek's hand and walked away whole. The Shek still talk about the manners.
I hear someone carried something to the Kingdom for a Shek who can't. That's a nasty errand and he did it.
A /FLATSKIN/ returned leather to the Kingdom. They didn't kill him.
Somebody took a debt to the Shek for a stranger. They say it was taken without a word. That's good with the Shek.
Skeletons read anything you hand them, I hear.
A Tech Hunter paid a man to carry a page to a skeleton once. Said he wouldn't touch it himself. He wasn't joking, I think.
Old paper from the ruins is more trouble than it's worth. Nobody can read it and nobody wants to be seen with it.
I never trusted a page that was written by someone who is dead. They write as if they will be read.
A page off a dead man is still a page.
The ruins give up paper more easily than coin. Paper is worse.
You find a lot of writing in the old places. Most of it's just lists.
I do not read old script. I know a few who do.
We read and aren't thanked for it. That isn't a complaint.
Paper does not last. We last.
We were given a page once. It was almost nothing.
Writing is a way to be found. Most of it isn't found.
A page was read to a stranger and the stranger left.
A traveller took a reading and left. That is the usual pattern.
We read for a stranger recently. No payment.
A page now belongs to us. It was not stolen. It was left.
I hear someone found a use for a dead man's page. I'd like it to have been me.
A page changed hands and nobody was killed. That is odd.
Somebody did a hunter's errand and didn't ask for double. I'd like to know them.
A hunter got his reading and it cost him only a fair price.
I knew a slaver who paid a man's way home and called it a loss on the books.
Everyone in this trade has a column they don't look at.
The trade doesn't forgive. The trade only forgets, for a price.
You can hear a man come to hate his work. It sounds like very careful accounting.
They say the anti-slaver ninjas take coin from anyone who doesn't ask for anything back.
Coins turn up at the ninjas from strange hands. They don't ask whose.
I don't mind who gives, so long as they don't want thanks. Thanks cost more than coin.
Money is money. It doesn't know where it has been.
Slavers feel nothing, so I hear. The ones I knew felt plenty. They billed it elsewhere.
A slaver once gave me bread. I took it. I didn't thank him. I didn't forget it either.
A coin can be a bribe, a payment or an apology. You can only tell by what the hand does after.
People are bought and sold in this world, and the people doing it still go home to supper.
Somebody carried coin out of a slave shop to the other side. Nobody says whose. The books are quiet on it.
One of us paid a debt in the wrong direction. I admire it. I won't be copying it.
I hear a coin went missing and then turned up in the right place. Don't look for the thief.
The trade lost one coin and gained a clean conscience for a dealer.
A slaver's coin reached us. It was bent. I don't know what to make of it.
They say a trader sent us money from his own pocket. It isn't much. It's something.
We have coin from the trade now and we're using it against the trade.
A bent coin, a stranger, a message. Not many messages come our way that don't mean a fight.
The Mongrel will have anyone, they say, so long as you can fight or fool somebody.
Half the families in the Cities have someone they don't speak of. Gone to the bandits, gone to the sand. You learn to stop looking up the road.
I knew a man who wrote to his brother every year. He never got an answer.
A letter is the most dangerous thing you can carry. It can make a person turn around.
A note came in once, years back. A man read it twice and left in the night.
Everyone here left someone. We don't talk of it.
A message from home is a bad omen or a good one. You can't tell until you read it.
I once burned a letter unread. I think about it more than I should.
I had a cousin who went to the Mongrel. We didn't write. I think we should have.
Gone is gone. But a note doesn't know that.
Some of the lost aren't dead. They're only elsewhere, which is harder.
I heard a man can disappear into a crowd of the worst sort and remember his mother's name for years.
A note came to a stranger who carried it in, and a man here read it and sat down. I won't say who.
Someone got a letter from home. They've been quiet since.
A sealed note came and went. It left an odd mood.
A man has been looking at his hands all day. A letter came. I know nothing.
A woman I know looks lighter lately. She won't say why.
I heard a note went out to a relation among the rough crowd. I hope it was welcome.
One of ours sent a message to a lost one. It's a brave thing and a hard one.
Somebody finally sent that note. It took long enough.
A gate sergeant took a smuggler's purse and waved him in. The smuggler came back with friends. The sergeant doesn't stand at that gate now.
People say the Cities guards have a price. They say it sadly, as if it were weather.
Slip a tired guard a few cats and he forgets how to read. Slip it to a rested one and you forget how to walk.
A man bribed his way in at one gate and got robbed at the next. Nobody sold him a map of honest ones.
Two thousand for a patrol to look away. A few hundred for a sergeant at a gate. Cheap, until it isn't.
A gate guard turned in his own captain for taking coin. They made him sergeant, then posted him somewhere worse.
Some Cities guards cannot be bought. They are the ones who get posted to the dull towns.
I offered a patrolman a purse. He wrote my name down and asked me to spell it. I don't go to that gate now.
There's an honest guard at the south gate. Nobody has found his price. Several have gone broke looking.
A bribe is a gamble. Half the guards eat it. The other half eat you.
A paladin took a tithe to forget a pack. They say he was the one who turned my cousin in a month later.
The Flame can't be bought. A paladin on a bad month can be rented.
There are frightened men in the Nation's helmets. Frightened men look at the floor, if you ask them to.
A priest once let a smuggler pass for a donation. The temple got the cats. The priest got a cell.
Paladins are paid in prayer. Prayer doesn't buy bread.
A man tried to buy his way past a paladin in the city. They burned the bag. They didn't stop at the bag.
The holy ones despise bribes. Not the ones who offer, the ones who accept.
I would sooner swim the swamp than hand a Nation guard a coin.
Try buying a paladin and learn the colour of a cage.
Don't offer. In the Nation, offering is the crime they were waiting for.
Offer a Shek a bribe and learn what a flatskin's hand is worth. It isn't much, in pieces.
The Shek don't take coin to look away. Take it as a warning, not as a rumour.
I saw a flatskin try to bribe a Shek gate guard. He's still on his knees. He's very polite now.
A Shek called bribery the worst of crimes. He didn't say what was the second worst.
Strange kingdom. No tolls, no bribes. Only the blade, and then the apology.
Two thousand to look away at a patrol. A few hundred at a gate. Fifty if the guard is lazy and the night is long.
A guard takes your money depending on his mood. You don't learn his mood until you try.
Honest guards cost you nothing, and so much more. Crooked guards cost you cats, and still might not do it.
Never bribe the nervous ones in front of the sergeant. Nervous ones remember the sergeant.
Some take it. Some report you. Some do both, in that order.
They ask for coin if you carry nothing. They ask for everything if you carry a pack.
The Dust Bandits count your backpacks before they count your cats. A bag is an admission.
Three hundred is an insult to a bandit with a good eye. They know what a pack can hide.
Carry the bag, lose the bag. Leave it behind, lose a few hundred.
Bandits aren't stupid. A big pack and a small purse tells them a story, and they don't like the ending.
Reavers charge by how heavy you look. I walked the coast with nothing on my back once. It cost me my boots.
The Reavers never take the first offer. They take the second, and the third, until there is no fourth.
Pay the road gangs early and light. Let them think you're poor. They won't believe you, but they'll remember the courtesy.
Pay the road gangs early and light. They won't believe you're poor, but they remember the courtesy.
The hungry ones ask for food first. Cats when they have no food to ask for. Nothing when they have neither.
A man with no pack told a starving bandit he had nothing. They shared a long silence and parted friends.
Starvers don't set tolls. They set a mood. Meet it, and keep walking.
Never joke with a hungry bandit about your lunch. Only one of you'll be laughing, and it won't be him.
A woman out without her husband or brother gets noticed here. Noticed is the best you can hope for.
They restrict the women here. You get used to it. You stop noticing the quiet.
The priests say women are Narko's image. The priests are men. Make of that what you will.
Rumour has it a woman walked into the temple unescorted last month. She isn't mentioned any more.
Stay in, stay veiled, stay quiet. It's simpler than the alternative.
I've heard of women purged for stepping out without an escort. I've never asked what happened to the escort.
A woman's best protection here's a man who doesn't mind answering for her.
The Inquisitors check women first. That's how they find the tainted ones, people say.
If you must walk with a woman, stay close, speak first, and hope she says nothing.
Never take a woman north without a man beside her. The Nation doesn't ask questions. It doesn't need to.
A friend went into the Holy Nation with her husband. She came back. He didn't. That's how they do it.
I heard in the Nation a woman is punished for walking alone. They're right.
The Holy Nation punishes women who travel without a male escort. Most only fear it.
The Nation despises women who read, women who fight, and women who walk unescorted.
If you're a woman, and you must pass through the Holy Nation, find a man, or find another road.
I heard women flee the Nation for Flotsam. Not many reach it.
A woman in the Nation is a guest of whoever claims her. Claim yourself first, and walk away.
Fallen out with the Anti-Slavers? There's a pacifier in Mud Town. Bring a great many cats.
Mud Town is where you buy the Anti-Slavers back.
The man in Mud Town can talk the Anti-Slavers round. Your purse does the real talking.
Mud Town sells forgiveness for the Anti-Slavers. Dear, but cheaper than a cage.
They say the Anti-Slavers' peacemaker sits in Mud Town. They are usually right about the price.
The Hounds hold grudges. The Hub holds a pacifier for them.
Wronged the Hounds? Go to the Hub and pay someone who talks gently.
There's a man in the Hub who makes the Hounds forget. For a fee.
Hounds don't forgive. Hounds are paid to. The Hub is where.
The Hub has a pacifier for the Hounds. It's on the same street as the people who need one.
The Shek have a pacifier at World's End. It costs less than your head.
Cross the Shek? World's End has someone who mends that. Bring cats, not excuses.
They say a flatskin can buy peace with the Shek in World's End. A Shek would never say so.
World's End. The Shek peace is sold there. Strange, for a people with no use for coin.
The slavers keep a pacifier at Stoat. Odd to pay slavers for peace. Odder not to.
If the slavers want you, Stoat has a man who talks them out of it.
Pay the slave traders at Stoat and they forget your face. They never forget the price.
Stoat. That's where the slavers mend their quarrels.
The Cities angry at you? Flats Lagoon has a pacifier. Pay the fee, forget the fines.
Flats Lagoon will clear your name with the Cities. A very long ledger, a very short list of ways.
If the Empire wants you, go to Flats Lagoon with a heavy purse.
A man in Flats Lagoon sells you back to the Cities. Think of it as a loan.
A pacifier costs a fortune. A bounty costs your head.
There is a man for every faction who will fix a bad name. They all want paying. Heavily.
The pacifier does not care who you killed. Only that you can pay for forgetting.
I saved for years to be forgiven. I spent it in one afternoon. I'd do it again.
Pay the Nation for peace? Repentance is the only coin the Flame takes.
No man sells forgiveness here. Forgiveness is paid in prayer, and in ash.
A bounty with the Nation is settled in the cells or on the pyre. Nobody has found a third way.
The Nation forgives the penitent. The penitent don't come back to ask the price.
The Shinobi keep a hut in most big towns. Heng, Catun, Heft. Ask for a quiet man.
Looking for the thieves? They keep a place in the larger towns. Heng has one, I'm told.
Join the Shinobi and the guards stop being your problem. Mostly.
Catun, Heft, Heng. Every one has a back door with nobody guarding it.
Thieves don't advertise. Look for the place the guards avoid looking at.
The Shinobi sell membership like a stall sells bread.
They take cats at the door. Plenty of them. After that, you're a brother.
Thieves stick together. That costs more than sticking alone.
Joining the Shinobi costs a great deal. Not joining costs your pockets, now and then.
Thieves? There are no thieves in the Cities. Ask somebody else, and ask quietly.
I would never point a stranger toward that sort of place. I would not know where it was, either.
The Empire's law has an answer for people who ask. You won't like it.
Go and ask the guards. I'm sure they'll be curious why you want to know.
No. And I didn't hear the question.
A den of sinners. I wouldn't name it, and I'll report whoever does.
Seek the thieves and the Flame will find you first.
There's no such place in Okran's land. If there were, I'd burn it.
Ask me that again and the Inquisitors will ask you why.
Pray for your own sake that you didn't mean what you said.
Flatskin thieves and their holes. A Shek has no use for either.
Ask a flatskin. I don't keep company with shadows.
A thief is a coward with quick hands. I won't tell you where to find them.
No. A Shek doesn't lead anyone to a thieves' nest.
Go and ask the rats. They know.
Black Desert City has the best robot limbs in the land. Taken off dead Skeletons, I hear.
Need a new leg? Black Desert City. Mind the sand, mind the twisters, mind your boots.
The Skeletons sell parts in Black Desert City. Used parts. Very used.
The robotics shop in Black Desert City is the best anywhere. The road there's the price.
Mongrel sells robot legs. Plenty of demand. Mind the fog on the way.
Legs in Mongrel. Everyone there seems to need them. Do not ask why.
For a limb that works, go to Mongrel. For a limb that fits, bring patience.
Mongrel is where legs go when they've lost their owners. Cheap enough, if you can stand the fog.
The Hivers sell cheap legs. Cheap, I said.
Need a leg and short of cats? The hive will sell you one. It won't look good.
A hive limb gets you walking. It does not get you admired.
The hive grows its own. It will sell you spares. Don't ask what they're made of.
Machine limbs are an abomination. I won't tell you where to buy one. Wear one here, and you'll burn.
Ask about iron legs in the Nation and see how the street empties.
Cut off by the Skeleton wars and fitted with metal? Don't come here.
There's an iron foot in a ditch outside the walls. Its owner was found nearby.
Parts come from the Black Desert, or from Mongrel. Or from whatever stops moving first.
I need a limb. A limb needs a donor. Donors are scarce, and often unwilling.
Spare parts are spare. Most of mine were somebody's.
A limb is a limb. Whose it was isn't my concern.
Hurt? Any big town has someone with a needle and a bottle. Ask the barman, he has stitches of his own.
A doctor is easy to find. A good one is easy to afford, or neither.
Skeletons need robot repair, the rest of us need a doctor. The doctor is easier to find.
If you bleed in a town, someone will sew you up. If you bleed outside, bleed quietly.
Catun has the most famous weapon smith. Heng has one of the best shops around. Both are worth the walk.
A good blade is from Catun. A better argument is from Heng. Take your pick.
For weapons, Catun and Heng. For anything else, the nearest gutter.
A Catun blade is good. A Heng blade is better. A blade from neither is a rumour.
The Scraphouse in Black Desert City beats every weapon shop in the land. Getting there's the real test.
Best weapons are in Black Desert City. Worst road in the world to carry them back along.
A Scraphouse blade is a rumour I trust. I've seen what's left of the ones who bought one.
Scraphouse. Say the word and watch a tinker go quiet.
Heft is the best place I found for armour. I cannot think of any other, unless you count the rumour about the Armour King.
Good plate comes from Heft. Everything else is a story.
If you want to stay alive, buy armour in Heft. If you want to stay in coins, don't.
Armour from Heft. Everything else I have bought has been a lesson.
For crossbows, the Tech Hunter towns. Mongrel too, if you don't mind the fog. Black Scratch is good.
The Tech Hunters make decent crossbows. They'll tell you so.
A crossbow out of Black Scratch has never failed me. I have never tested it on anything that fights back.
Heard Mongrel has a decent crossbow maker. Heard the fog has a better one.

Forbidden pages, they say, and older than the Holy Nation. I keep my eyes on the scripture I am given.
My mother said the saviour had an older name. She said it once. She didn't say it twice.

Some pages the Nation burned were worth the burning.

A martyr, a god, a machine, a rumour. The Holy Nation won't say which, and that tells me enough.

The priests say we were made human once. Say it to a horn and see what comes back.
Before Kral we don't speak. Humans make up the rest.

Word is, something made us. I say something broke our teachers and we did the rest.

Humans, Shek. The horns don't change what's under them. We're slow to notice differences.
The horned ones are gentle with us, when they aren't hitting us. I don't understand it.
Created human, the book says. I've never been sure what that means for them.

Priests say horns came late. Shek say priests came late. I bet on the horns.

Venge is bad in daylight. Walk it at night, if you walk it.
Something up there still works. The old ones swear to it. Something up there also stopped. They swear to that too.
I don't cross Venge. The ground is bare as a skull, and not from the wind.

Burn marks on the old stone, the long kind, from above. The books don't agree what made them.

Something over the Eye stopped working. I remember the quiet more than the work.
One of them stopped. I think. A memory, or a story I was told.
Don't stand under the light in Venge. I can't tell you how I know.
Some quiet is the end of something. The Eye is that kind of quiet.

There are zones on the map nobody sells guides to. Venge is the first one the guild skips.
The east burns by itself. We call it a tax on travel. The scholars call it unknown.
Nobody mines Venge. The ore is fine. The sky is the problem.

There were ports where there's only dust. I'm not sure it's a memory.
People loved their boats once. I think I'm fond of them for no reason.

The coast was further in. The scholars measure it and look ill.
The shore moved. We have the maps and the shame.
Old hands say there was a harbour out in the muck once. Boats in a bog.
The swamp had water before it had weeds. Some of us can feel it, some of us are just drunk.
Old Swamper told me the muck was a bay once. He also told me the moon was a bad egg.
Boats in the bog. Somebody believed in them once.
The old folk say the water stood higher. They say a lot. They're usually right about the weather.
I found a hull on a hill once. I didn't stay to ask how it got up there.
Old hulls sit far from any water. The old folk shrug.
Used to be more water, they say. Used to be a lot of things.

Drought, then famine, then the guild caravans that never came. Rogues on the roads, so I hear.
The nobles took what rations came and locked the doors. I'd have done the same, and I won't forgive myself for saying so.
We don't speak of the Rebellion near an official. We speak of the weather.
Don't look at the nobles. Don't look at their windows. My mother looked once, in the Rebellion.
They locked the gates and let us starve. We haven't forgotten. We haven't said so, either.
The laws got harder after. Nobody tells you which laws.
The red year taught us two things. Don't say what you saw, and don't be hungry near a noble.
The Empire starved its own and called the survivors criminals. We just call them neighbours.
Nobles bidding over grain while the poor ate each other. Good riddance to the rule they made.
Half the swamp came from somewhere the Rebellion burned.
The Empire fed its nobles and fined its poor. Then it was surprised.
My folk had a farm before the red year. Now we have a road and a knife. Fair trade, nobody asked.
They called us rebels. We were hungry. The words don't mean the same thing.
The Rebellion wasn't a war. It was a very large mistake that people had to die of.
Lady Tanaka wrote it down. She was the one who shut the gate.
Heathens killing each other over cats and bread. Okran was not mocked.
The Empire ate itself in the red year. We watched from the hills and said nothing, as scripture teaches.
The Empire fought itself over bread. Okran has no use for such weakness.
Okran watched the Empire starve and wasn't surprised.
Humans starve over coin. Some say our kind raided the aid wagons. Nobody admits it. Nobody asks a Shek twice.
The Empire starved because humans would rather hoard than share. We saw it. We did not stop it.
Rogues blocked the aid wagons, so I hear. Some had horns. We don't discuss it.
The red year was human business. Our business is the sword.

Memory is a thing you carry until it breaks. Then you stop carrying it. Don't look at me like that.
I could recall more. I choose not to.

Ask a skeleton about the old world and he goes quiet. Not the polite quiet either.
They wiped something at some point, long long ago. Skeletons won't say what.
Skeletons forget. We remember being told. It isn't the same, and we pretend it is.
The First Extinction was the darkness's doing. The saviour cleansed the world and the faithful alone endured.
Darkness caused the First Extinction. The Second is coming. That isn't a threat, it's the scripture.
The light was betrayed once. It won't be betrayed twice. That's why we stand watch.
The First Extinction came from darkness. The Second will come from the same, and we'll be ready.
The First Extinction? Plague, my colleague says. A weapon, says the colleague down the hall. We share a roof and not a conclusion.
Whatever ended the old world left no witnesses and a great many theories. Theories are cheap. Digging is dear.
One thing every scholar agrees on. It was quick.
Plague, weapon, flood. A scholar for each. Not one of them has been to the right ruin.
Humans cry about cities that drowned. Warriors do not dwell on what is gone.
The old world ended. So will this one. A warrior meets it standing.
The old world fell. Warriors stood. That is the whole story.
Cities drowned. Our people were not there to see. Good.
Big Hunger come. /CANNIBALHA/ Ate all. Some still eating.
Old world have big hunger. Dhey eat dhemselves. /CANNIBALHA/. We learned from dhem.
Big Hunger take many. We take dhe rest. /CANNIBALHA/
Old world full. Dhen empty. Now we fill it. /CANNIBALHA/
Every old family in the Cities has a grandfather who walked here from somewhere worse. Don't ask which somewhere.
We left when leaving was still possible. That's the only founding story I trust.
The Cities weren't planned. They were what was left standing when people stopped believing in the old throne.
My family doesn't say where it came from. It says it arrived, and that's enough pride for one table.
Narko lies beneath the roots, hidden from the light, tempting the weak. That's why the faithful don't trust the old trees.
The darkness was thrown into the abyss under the roots of the trees. Don't forget it when you walk at night.
Okran cast his dark half down so it could do no harm. The dark half has been patient ever since.
Every soul must conquer the darkness within, as Okran did. I try each morning.
Okran warms and Narko cools. Ask the Holy Nation which one it burns in.
Heretic is a word the frightened use for the faithful they can't control.
Narko is the half they threw away.
The light and the dark are the same hand, they say. We believe it with some caution.
Plenty pray to both the light and the dark. Only the Holy Nation insists on one and burns people over it.
A god of day, a goddess of night. I pray to both. Just in case.
The Okranites hate the dark and fear the roots. I fear the Okranites, which is more practical.
Many pray to both. Only the Holy Nation insists on one.
People need a shadow to blame. We've been cast as the villain for longer than I can remember.
Agents of darkness, they call us. I'd like to see the contract.
Narko, Narko. There's always a villain, and we always fit the costume.
The shadow, they call us. We never asked to be a story.
Light and dark taste dhe same. /CANNIBALHA/
Dhe holy ones say big dark under dhe trees. We sleep dhere. /CANNIBALHA/ Still ungry.
Dhe holy ones fear dhe roots. We fear dhe holy ones. /CANNIBALHA/
Dark under dhe trees? We dig dhere.
Kral died with a hundred swords around him and passed to Gateway. A warrior asks no better.
Only a warrior's death opens Gateway. I don't talk about dying old. It's a wound that doesn't close.
There are fewer of us every year. The ones who go, go well.
A man who lost his horns still carries Kral's name. He carries my pack too. That's the order of things.
My knees know the weather. I don't ask my years. It shames a warrior to be counted that high.
I should have gone at Kral's side. I'm still here. That's the hard part.
Dying in bed is for flatskins. I'm too slow for the other way.
I counted my years once. I won't do it again.
A pagan cult of beasts. Their glory is throwing themselves away. The Flame can help them find it.
They worship a corpse called Kral and call the afterlife Gateway. Gateway will have no room for them.
Their Gateway has no gate. It has a pyre. The Flame is happy to provide.
Cult of beasts. A Shek who dies well meets us at the Flame.
A warrior cult that keeps throwing itself away. Good for business. There are always fewer of them.
Shek talk of dying well as other men talk of dinner. Don't join the conversation.
Honour is a fine sentiment for a customer who pays up front. The Shek do neither.
A people that keeps dying on purpose.
Dying for a name is an old habit of the living. We say nothing, and we listen.
Dying for a name is an old habit of the living.
Honour, glory, Gateway. The living need such words. We let them have them.
I've watched many march to a good death. I've never learned to clap.
A warrior dies well, they say.
We know no-hive that walked out of the hum. This one doesn't look at them long.
The quiet after the hum is the worst. No-hive say they hear nothing.
When the hum is gone, a hiver stops. Some of us walk. Some of us don't know why we walk.
We were taught not to speak of the ones who lost the hum. We speak of them anyway, softly.
Met a hiver once, alone, no hive. He kept pausing mid-sentence, like listening to a door.
The ones who lost the hum, bug men call them. They stop talking in the middle of words.
A hiver without a hive is a bad bargain and a sadder story.
One of them stood in a field once, as if waiting for a call.
Hivers get quiet when their kin get lost. Not sad quiet.
Ask a hiver about the queen and the room changes. Nobody has ever seen her. Nobody wants to be the one to say so.
Bug men don't discuss the queen. They discuss weather. It means the same thing.
A hiver goes quiet when he hears the hum is gone. I've seen it.
Don't look at them. Don't say the word. It's the Vault. That's all I'll say, and too much.
Enemies of the nobility go to the Vault. Nobody describes it. That's the whole description.
A cousin went to the Vault. We don't set a place for him. We don't say his name.
Emperor Tengu
Nobody gets out of Tengu's Vault. A man who says otherwise is selling something.
The Vault takes rebels and keeps them. We take our own risks and keep them too.
You can be hung for less than what they do in the Vault. That's the nicest thing I can say about it.
We don't talk about the Vault.
The nobles built a place for people like us. We built a place for people like them.
Half the people we pull out of chains have heard of the Vault. None of them have seen it.
Emperor Tengu
Tengu's Vault. There's a name that makes a tired man sit up.
We have emptied a lot of cages. The Vault is the one door we haven't found.
Whatever is in the Vault, the people who left it won't say.
Don't breathe near the nobles. They say there's a torture Vault for rebels and anyone else who irritates them.
If you hear screaming near Skimsands, you didn't hear it.
Don't mention the Vault where nobles can hear. Don't mention it where their servants can hear either.
Skimsands is quiet. That's how you know where the Vault is.
